description: Applies the FSharp.Refactor analyzers' quick fixes to F# code from the command line. Point it at a project, a script, a solution, a directory or a glob; --dry-run reports without editing. The tool clarifies the (agent-generated or old) code's intent, reduces non-alphanumeric noise, and uses built-in .NET libraries more efficiently.
releaseNotes:
0.8.29: FR0172 (idiom, fix): a match arm that binds a whole list only to read `itms.[0]` (or `itms[0]`, `itms.Head`, `List.head itms`), `itms.[1]` or `itms.Tail` is a cons pattern - `| itms -> g itms.[0]` becomes `| itmsHead :: _ -> g itmsHead`, the tail named only where the arm reads it. Exact where an earlier unguarded `[]` arm (and `[_]` for a second element) already keeps the short lists out of the arm, so the match stays as complete as it was and the compiler's exhaustiveness check stands in for the ArgumentException a list index raises; any other use of the name, an index above 1, a rebinding inside the arm, or an array (`[||]`) or an earlier bare catch-all (which covers every array and string too) stands the rule down. Parse-only, the `[]` arm settling the type. Measured: no run-time difference between the shapes - `xs.[0]` walks no cells - so the rule is the idiom, not speed. FR0156 takes the `let mutable` list beside the ResizeArray: `let mutable xs = []` fed by `xs <- xs @ [ e ]` or `List.append xs [ e ]` inside its loops and only read after becomes the list expression with each element as its yield (measured at 1000 elements: 250x faster on 0.3% of the allocation - every append copied the list), and `xs <- e :: xs` read through `List.rev` alone does too, the reverse becoming the bare name (1.5x on half); an assignment after the loops, a read inside them, a list fed at both ends or a project's own `@` stands it down. FR0050 leaves that combine alone (a fold would keep the copy), and FR0051's note names the list expression first. PerfClaims gains the cases FR0168, FR0170 and FR0171 had not got; FR0171's runs long enough to tier up, since a byte string literal is `InitializeArray` from RVA data, a helper call at tier 0 and a copy at tier 1. FR0071 now leaves an array literal inside the loop where it still hoists a list: a list is immutable, so n allocations become one and nothing can tell, but an array literal is a fresh mutable buffer per iteration and a hoisted one is shared by every pass. FR0015 per-call hoist knob: { "FR0015": { "perCall": false } } keeps the loop hoists and leaves a Regex in a plain function body where it is written; on by default, since a function is far likelier to be called many times than a module is to be initialised with its hoisted binding never read.

 0.8.28: A guard and rule exchange with CSharp.Refactor, twin by twin. Guards: FR0004 proves the source pure before a consumer that stops early (`exists`, `find`, `head`) - `Seq.exists` over a `seq { }` with an effect would skip some of it; FR0016 and FR0070 refuse a struct the file boxes, locks or null-tests, one implementing an interface, or one over 32 bytes inline (four decimals copy slower than they allocate); FR0075 and FR0032 pass over `HttpClient`, `HttpRequestMessage` and its contents, `SemaphoreSlim`, `ManualResetEventSlim` and `Task` (no resource the scope owns, and a handler mock reads the request back after the send); FR0151 knows `AggregateException` (InnerExceptions), `SqlException` (Number) and `FileNotFoundException` (FileName); FR0037's HttpClient note and FR0165 stand down in test files; FR0142 accepts TUnit. FR0015 hoists a Regex from any function body, not only a loop - a function is called from loops the file cannot see, and a construction is parsed per call. Fixes: FR0118's unobserved loop gains `ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` as its first statement; FR0164's filter shape becomes the list's own `RemoveAll`. Four rules: FR0168 (performance, fix) `try T.Parse s with _ -> 0` is `match T.TryParse s with`, a sweep applying it where the catch covers everything TryParse answers false to, FR0055 standing down there; FR0169 (correctness, note) a `seq` parameter or local enumerated twice on one path; FR0170 (performance, fix) `for k in d.Keys do ... d.[k]` is `for KeyValue(k, v) in d do`; FR0171 (performance, fix) `Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes "OK"` is `"OK"B`.

 0.8.27: Seven correctness rules, the F# twins of CSharp.Refactor's CR0160-CR0171 family where F# does not rule the hazard out by design. FR0159: `float (sum / count)` divides as integers before it widens - the editor offers `float sum / float count`, a sweep never applies it, and a literal operand or a product dividend (`float (screenW / 2)`, `float (x * mw / tw)`: a pixel centre, a scaled coordinate) is the editor's alone unless `{ "FR0159": { "all": true } }`. FR0160: a handler raising a new exception without the one it caught gains it as the constructor's trailing argument where the type has that constructor (`raise (X("m", ex))`, a `_`/`:? T` pattern gaining `as ex`); `failwith` in a handler that never reads what it caught is a note. FR0161: a mutating method on the struct a property returns mutates a copy - the one such copy F# does not refuse at compile time. FR0162: check-then-assign on a module-level or `static let` mutable races; `lazy` runs the factory once. FR0163: a `System.Threading.Timer` nothing references is collected mid-flight (a `System.Timers.Timer` is not - measured). FR0164: a collection edited inside a `for` over itself throws at the next step; the loop walks `Array.ofSeq items`. FR0165: a local `DateTime` compared with or subtracted from a UTC one flips with the timezone. Three rules widen: FR0055 notes the narrow catch that is TryParse as control flow (`with :? FormatException -> 0`) and offers the rewrite where the catch covers what TryParse turns into false; FR0118 notes an awaiting loop under a token that never observes it; FR0123 notes `SemaphoreSlim.Wait`/`ReaderWriterLockSlim.Enter*Lock`/`Mutex.WaitOne` with no `finally` release and, where the release is a statement of the same block, moves the statements between under a `try` and the release into its `finally`. Every gate the C# side learned on real repositories came along - a mutation in a lambda is deferred, a store under `lock gate <| fun () ->` is guarded, an `IList<_>` may be concurrent, a compound emptiness test is a reconnecting holder, not a lazy - and a dry run over fourteen projects of the corpus proposed no fix and no false note. The property suite now typechecks what it generates: eleven rule families of shapes over a two-file script (a stub declares the test-framework and logger namespaces some rules gate on), four properties over every family at once, a per-shape check that each shape reaches its rule - or, for a shape spelled `!FR0162`, that the rule stays quiet on it, the false-positive guard a real repository taught - and a catalog test that every rule has a shape or a stated reason none can. It found three defects: FR0065's whole-setting comment-out put the comment before the `()` and moved the block's offside column, FR0080 read a string literal inside a block comment as code where the compiler stays in the comment, and the shared test-file marker did not know `[<TestCaseSource>]`. FR0012 no longer withholds the `isNull` hint beside a boolean operator: the named-argument guard took every parent application for a call, `||` included, so `x = null || flag` was never rewritten while `if x = null` was; an operator application is not a call, and the replacement stands bare there (`isNull x || flag`). The Visual Studio extension's tagger constructs `FrTagger` with `new`, as FS0760 asks. Two performance rules and a wider FR0106, all gated on a modern framework (the compilation's String must offer its char and span overloads, so netstandard2.0 and net4x passes stay quiet): FR0106 also rewrites a Substring handed to StringBuilder.Append or TextWriter.Write; FR0166 turns a prefix or suffix cut out to compare with a literal into StartsWith/EndsWith with StringComparison.Ordinal (a slice everywhere, a Substring under a .Length guard); FR0167 walks the string itself where `for` or Array.iter/exists/forall read a ToCharArray copy once. FR0066 no longer reads an interpolation hole filled from a constant as a value; FR0127 reads `123456` as a made-up key. FR0015 takes CR0108's shapes: Match(...).Success and the Matches(...).Count tests become Contains (or the ordinal StartsWith), a literal Split becomes String.Split with the separator array.
 0.8.26: A property-based suite, `tests/FSharp.Refactor.PropertyTests`, joins the example-based one: FsCheck generates a module of declarations shaped for the parse-only rules, and boolean terms over three integers with an interpreter as the oracle, and the properties are the invariants the rules promise - a parse-only fix keeps the file parseable, no rule throws on a tree the parser recovered from damaged text, applying edits one at a time reaches a fixed point, and the boolean rewrites (FR0108/FR0109, the negation and De Morgan hints, FR0010, FR0013) keep the function's truth table at every step. It found one defect, shared by every rule that replaces a bracketed expression with a bare one: a replacement that begins or ends in an identifier character, put where the brackets were, runs into the token beside it - `match not (a <> b)with` is legal F#, and the hint's `a = b` left `bwith`. FR0012, FR0013, FR0094, FR0097, FR0098, FR0108 and FR0109 now put one space on the side that would glue, and none anywhere else. The FR0012 purity probe reads an interpolated string part by its case rather than a catch-all, so a part the parser adds later cannot pass as literal text.
 0.8.25: Every help link names the rule's own section of Rules.md: the SARIF rule metadata and the HTML report link to `Rules.md#fr0103--idiom`, the anchor GitHub gives the `### FR0103 — idiom` heading, where a bare `#fr0103` lands on nothing; a test slugs every heading the way GitHub does and holds the catalog's anchors against them. The Visual Studio extension's package lists a content type for every part again: manifest.json and catalog.json were written after the payload was enumerated, and a part without one made the whole file "not a valid VSIX package" once the FSAC payload's own .json files no longer hid it.
 0.8.24: The apply tool's build-configuration probe reads each compile item by the path the project spells. The item set is keyed by lowercased paths for membership, and the probe read the file through the key: on a case-sensitive file system `library.fs` is not `Library.fs`, an unreadable file counts as branching on the configuration, and on Linux every project got the extra Release pass and the extra Release build (the CI's consumer-verification test failed on the wording of a build it did not expect). The probe now reads the spelled path, and a test writes a project whose item's case the file system has to match. The wait on a child build no longer has the run at its mercy: after a `dotnet build` exits, the wait for its output pipes to close gets ten seconds, not forever, and the child runs with MSBuild node reuse off, since a worker node kept for the next build inherits the pipes and held the run - and the test host - for as long as it lived.
